what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat Pompe disease (also called acid maltase deficiency or glycogen storage disease type II) in patients who are at least 1 year old. Pompe disease causes a buildup of a sugar called glycogen in your muscles, which makes them weak over time. This medicine helps break down that extra glycogen so your muscles can work better.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion — meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle or catheter. It is always given by a healthcare provider in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. You should NOT try to give this medicine to yourself at home unless your doctor specifically trains you and approves home infusion. Each infusion typically takes about 4 hours or more, depending on your dose and how well you tolerate it.
dosing: The usual dose is 40 mg per kilogram (mg/kg) of your body weight, given once every 2 weeks. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose based on your weight. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss or skip an infusion appointment, call your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to miss doses, as skipping treatments can cause your Pompe disease symptoms to get worse. Do not try to give yourself a double dose to make up for a missed one.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by your healthcare team. If you are given any supplies to take home, keep the medicine refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in its original packaging and out of direct light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Discard any unused medicine as directed by your healthcare provider.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines, vitamins, herbal products, and supplements you take before starting this medicine, as some may interact with it. Avoid skipping infusion appointments. Do not receive live vaccines without talking to your doctor first. If you feel unwell or have signs of an allergic reaction during or after your infusion, tell your healthcare provider right away and do not ignore symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you have any of the following: trouble breathing or shortness of breath; chest pain or tightness; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; severe rash, hives, or itching; dizziness, fainting, or a fast heartbeat; fever or chills during or after your infusion; nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain that is severe; muscle weakness that suddenly gets worse; or any other unusual or severe symptoms. Infusion reactions can happen during or shortly after your IV drip — always let your nurse know immediately if something feels wrong.
when_it_works: This medicine works right away in your body to start breaking down glycogen, but it may take weeks to months before you notice improvements in muscle strength, breathing, or ability to walk. Everyone responds differently. Keep attending all your scheduled infusions and follow-up appointments so your doctor can monitor your progress. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor, even if you do not notice changes right away.
special_populations: Children: This medicine is approved for children 1 year of age and older. Dosing is based on body weight. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not fully known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy or passes into breast milk, so talk with your doctor about the risks and benefits. Older adults: There is limited information about use in adults over 65. Talk to your doctor about any special considerations. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how your body handles the medicine.
